CALIFORNIA PAID SICK LEAVE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

ABOUT THIS CALIFORNIA PAID SICK LEAVE INFORMATION SHEET
This California Paid Sick Leave — Information Sheet describes California's statewide paid sick leave law, the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act of 2014 (Labor Code §§ 245-249), as it relates to the working relationship between Jordan Alex Lee and Acme Corp. It summarizes selected requirements of that law: who accrues paid sick leave and how, the alternative ways an employer may satisfy the accrual requirement, the statute's own permitted reasons for using paid sick leave, its definition of "family member" for that purpose, its anti-retaliation protection, its workplace-posting and recordkeeping duties, and the categories of workers the statute's own definitions exclude from coverage.

This document goes further into the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act than the brief references to paid sick leave already found elsewhere in this project's forms. The Vacation/PTO Payout at Termination document's sick-leave-distinction clause cites a single subsection of the Act — § 246(g)(1) — for the narrow point that accrued sick leave, unlike vacation, need not be paid out at termination; this document does not re-argue that point, but builds on it with the statute's own rehire-reinstatement exception, which that existing clause identifies as outside its own scope. The Wage Theft Prevention Act Notice to Employee document lists "paid sick leave rights" as one of several categories of information a hiring-time notice under a different statute (Labor Code § 2810.5) must contain; it does not describe the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act's own, separate workplace-posting requirement, which this document addresses directly as a distinct statutory duty from that hiring-time notice.

This information sheet is not itself the poster Labor Code § 247 requires an employer to display, does not itself compute or verify any specific amount of accrued or available paid sick leave for Jordan Alex Lee, and does not determine that any particular policy of Acme Corp's is or is not compliant with California law.

THE HEALTHY WORKPLACES, HEALTHY FAMILIES ACT AND ITS RELATIONSHIP TO OTHER RIGHTS
California's statewide paid sick leave statute is codified at Labor Code §§ 245 through 249 and states, in its own text, that it "shall be known and may be cited as the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act of 2014." The statute also states, in its own text, that its provisions are in addition to and independent of any other legal rights, remedies, or procedures available under any other law, and that the Act does not diminish, alter, or negate those other rights, remedies, or procedures.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This article shall be known and may be cited as the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act of 2014."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 245(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act, short title (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=245.)
  "The provisions of this article are in addition to and independent of any other rights, remedies, or procedures available under any other law and do not diminish, alter, or negate any other legal rights, remedies, or procedures available to an aggrieved person."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 245(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, non-exclusivity of other rights and remedies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=245.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's paid-sick-leave law and its own stated relationship to other legal rights — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation; a majority of states have no equivalent statewide paid-sick-leave mandate at all. Both citations below are to subdivisions (a) and (b) of a single statutory section, Section 245; they are treated here as one source describing the Act's title and its own non-exclusivity clause, not as independent corroborating sources. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself grant, calculate, or deny any specific amount of paid sick leave for any reader, and does not determine that any specific employer's policy is or is not compliant with the Act.

ACCRUAL RATE, THE ALTERNATIVE ACCRUAL AND UPFRONT-GRANT METHODS, AND THE ACCRUAL AND USAGE CAPS
Under Labor Code § 246, an employee who works for the same employer in California for 30 or more days within a year of the start of employment is entitled to paid sick days as the statute specifies. Absent a different method, an employee accrues paid sick days at a rate of not less than one hour for every 30 hours worked. The statute permits an employer to use a different accrual method instead, provided the accrual happens regularly enough that the employee has no less than 24 hours or 3 days of accrued sick leave (or paid time off usable for the same purposes) by the 120th calendar day of employment, or of each calendar year or 12-month period, and no less than 40 hours or 5 days by the 200th calendar day. Separately, an employer may satisfy the accrual requirement entirely by instead providing the statute's "full amount of leave" — defined as five days or 40 hours — up front, at the beginning of each year of employment, calendar year, or 12-month period, rather than through incremental accrual; where an employer does this, the statute does not require accrual or carryover. Where accrual instead applies, the statute lets an employer limit how much accrued paid sick leave an employee may use in a given year, calendar year, or 12-month period to 40 hours or five days, and separately lets an employer cap an employee's total banked accrual at no more than 80 hours or 10 days, so long as the employee's accrual and use rights are not otherwise limited beyond what the statute allows.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]

This section shall be satisfied and no accrual or carryover is required if the full amount of leave is received at the beginning of each year of employment, calendar year, or 12-month period. The term “full amount of leave” means five days or 40 hours."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 246(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, carryover, annual use limit, and upfront-grant alternative (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=246.)

PERMITTED REASONS FOR USING PAID SICK LEAVE
Labor Code § 246.5 requires an employer, upon an employee's oral or written request, to provide paid sick days for specified purposes. The first is diagnosis, care, or treatment of an existing health condition of, or preventive care for, the employee or the employee's family member. The second is use for a purpose described in other, separately cross-referenced statutes addressing leave connected to crime victimization and violence; as currently in effect, that cross-reference points to specified paragraphs of Government Code § 12945.8. The third, added for agricultural employees, permits use to avoid smoke, heat, or flooding conditions created by a proclaimed local or state emergency, including when the employee's worksite is closed because of those conditions. Government Code § 12945.8 in turn defines "qualifying act of violence," for these cross-referenced purposes, as including domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, and, more broadly, any act or pattern of conduct causing bodily injury or death, involving the exhibition or use of a firearm or other dangerous weapon, or involving an actual or threatened use of force to cause physical injury or death.

THE STATUTE'S DEFINITION OF "FAMILY MEMBER"
For purposes of using paid sick leave to care for someone other than the employee, Labor Code § 245.5 defines "family member" to mean a child (a biological, adopted, or foster child, a stepchild, a legal ward, or a child to whom the employee stands in loco parentis, regardless of the child's age or dependency status); a biological, adoptive, or foster parent, stepparent, or legal guardian of the employee or of the employee's spouse or registered domestic partner, or a person who stood in loco parentis when the employee was a minor child; a spouse; a registered domestic partner; a grandparent; a grandchild; a sibling; and a "designated person," defined as a person the employee identifies at the time the employee requests paid sick days, which an employer may limit to one designated person per 12-month period.

(2) A biological, adoptive, or foster parent, stepparent, or legal guardian of an employee or the employee’s spouse or registered domestic partner, or a person who stood in loco parentis when the employee was a minor child. (3) A spouse. (4) A registered domestic partner. (5) A grandparent. (6) A grandchild. (7) A sibling. (8) A designated person, which, for purposes of this article, means a person identified by the employee at the time the employee requests paid sick days. NO PAYOUT OF ACCRUED SICK LEAVE AT TERMINATION, WITH A REHIRE-REINSTATEMENT EXCEPTION
California's paid-sick-leave statute states directly that, except as specified in a rehire-reinstatement rule, an employer is not required to compensate an employee for accrued, unused paid sick days upon termination, resignation, retirement, or other separation from employment. The statute pairs that no-payout rule with the reinstatement rule itself: if an employee separates from an employer and is rehired by that same employer within one year of the date of separation, the employee's previously accrued and unused paid sick days must be reinstated, and the employee may use those reinstated days and continue accruing more, subject to the statute's usual use-and-accrual limits. The statute also states that an employer is not required to reinstate paid time off that was already paid out to the employee at the time of the earlier termination, resignation, or separation.

ANTI-RETALIATION PROTECTION FOR USING OR REQUESTING PAID SICK LEAVE
Labor Code § 246.5(c) prohibits an employer from denying an employee the right to use accrued sick days, or from discharging, threatening to discharge, demoting, suspending, or otherwise discriminating against an employee, for using accrued sick days, attempting to exercise the right to use them, filing a complaint alleging a violation of the statute, cooperating in an investigation or prosecution of an alleged violation, or opposing a policy, practice, or act the statute prohibits. The statute also creates a rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation where an employer denies the right to use accrued sick days, or discharges, threatens to discharge, demotes, suspends, or otherwise discriminates against an employee, within 30 days of that employee filing a complaint with the Labor Commissioner, cooperating with an investigation or prosecution of an alleged violation, or opposing a prohibited policy, practice, or act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer shall not deny an employee the right to use accrued sick days, discharge, threaten to discharge, demote, suspend, or in any manner discriminate against an employee for using accrued sick days, attempting to exercise the right to use accrued sick days, filing a complaint with the department or alleging a violation of this article, cooperating in an investigation or prosecution of an alleged violation of this article, or opposing any policy or practice or act that is prohibited by this article."

  "There shall be a rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation if an employer denies an employee the right to use accrued sick days, discharges, threatens to discharge, demotes, suspends, or in any manner discriminates against an employee within 30 days of any of the following: (A) The filing of a complaint by the employee with the Labor Commissioner or alleging a violation of this article. (B) The cooperation of an employee with an investigation or prosecution of an alleged violation of this article. (C) Opposition by the employee to a policy, practice, or act that is prohibited by this article."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 246.5(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=246.5.)

THE WORKPLACE-POSTING AND RECORDKEEPING DUTIES THIS ACT IMPOSES
Labor Code § 247 requires an employer to display, in a conspicuous place in each of its workplaces, a poster stating that an employee is entitled to accrue, request, and use paid sick days; the amount of sick days the Act provides; the terms of use of paid sick days; and that retaliation or discrimination against an employee who requests or uses paid sick days is prohibited, along with the employee's right to file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner. The statute directs the Labor Commissioner to create such a poster and make it available to employers, and states that an employer who willfully violates this posting requirement is subject to a civil penalty of not more than $100 per offense. Separately, Labor Code § 247.5 requires an employer to keep, for at least three years, records documenting the hours worked and the paid sick days accrued and used by an employee, to allow the Labor Commissioner access to those records, and to make them available to the employee in the same manner as other wage-statement-related records; if an employer does not maintain adequate records, the statute presumes the employee is entitled to the maximum number of accruable hours under the Act, unless the employer rebuts that presumption with clear and convincing evidence. Section 247.5 also states that, notwithstanding any other provision of the Act, an employer is not obligated to inquire into or record the specific purpose for which an employee uses paid leave or paid time off.

CATEGORIES OF WORKERS THE STATUTE'S OWN DEFINITIONS EXCLUDE
Labor Code § 245.5's definition of "employee," for purposes of this Act, excludes five categories of workers. The first is an employee covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement that expressly provides for wages, hours, and working conditions; expressly provides paid sick days (or a paid leave or paid time off policy permitting sick-day use) and final and binding arbitration of disputes over those provisions; and provides premium overtime rates and a regular hourly rate at least 30 percent above the state minimum wage — except that this exclusion does not reach the specific victim-of-violence-related permitted use described elsewhere in this Act. The second is a construction-industry employee covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement meeting similar wage and overtime conditions, where the agreement either predates January 1, 2015, or expressly and unambiguously waives this Act's requirements. The third is an air carrier flight deck or cabin crew member covered by Title II of the federal Railway Labor Act, so long as the individual receives compensated time off equal to or exceeding this Act's own default accrual amount. The fourth is a state or local public retiree drawing a retirement allowance who returns to work without reinstatement into the applicable public retirement system. The fifth is an employee as defined in a specified provision of the federal Railway Labor Act, 45 U.S.C. § 351(d).

expectedJSON.body: Under Labor Code § 246, an employee who works for the same employer in California for 30 or more days within a year of the start of employment is entitled to paid sick days as the statute specifies. Absent a different method, an employee accrues paid sick days at a rate of not less than one hour for every 30 hours worked. The statute permits an employer to use a different accrual method instead, provided the accrual happens regularly enough that the employee has no less than 24 hours or 3 days of accrued sick leave (or paid time off usable for the same purposes) by the 120th calendar day of employment, or of each calendar year or 12-month period, and no less than 40 hours or 5 days by the 200th calendar day. Separately, an employer may satisfy the accrual requirement entirely by instead providing the statute's "full amount of leave" — defined as five days or 40 hours — up front, at the beginning of each year of employment, calendar year, or 12-month period, rather than through incremental accrual; where an employer does this, the statute does not require accrual or carryover. Where accrual instead applies, the statute lets an employer limit how much accrued paid sick leave an employee may use in a given year, calendar year, or 12-month period to 40 hours or five days, and separately lets an employer cap an employee's total banked accrual at no more than 80 hours or 10 days, so long as the employee's accrual and use rights are not otherwise limited beyond what the statute allows.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code § 246.5 requires an employer, upon an employee's oral or written request, to provide paid sick days for specified purposes. The first is diagnosis, care, or treatment of an existing health condition of, or preventive care for, the employee or the employee's family member. The second is use for a purpose described in other, separately cross-referenced statutes addressing leave connected to crime victimization and violence; as currently in effect, that cross-reference points to specified paragraphs of Government Code § 12945.8. The third, added for agricultural employees, permits use to avoid smoke, heat, or flooding conditions created by a proclaimed local or state emergency, including when the employee's worksite is closed because of those conditions. Government Code § 12945.8 in turn defines "qualifying act of violence," for these cross-referenced purposes, as including domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, and, more broadly, any act or pattern of conduct causing bodily injury or death, involving the exhibition or use of a firearm or other dangerous weapon, or involving an actual or threatened use of force to cause physical injury or death.

expectedJSON.body: California's paid-sick-leave statute states directly that, except as specified in a rehire-reinstatement rule, an employer is not required to compensate an employee for accrued, unused paid sick days upon termination, resignation, retirement, or other separation from employment. The statute pairs that no-payout rule with the reinstatement rule itself: if an employee separates from an employer and is rehired by that same employer within one year of the date of separation, the employee's previously accrued and unused paid sick days must be reinstated, and the employee may use those reinstated days and continue accruing more, subject to the statute's usual use-and-accrual limits. The statute also states that an employer is not required to reinstate paid time off that was already paid out to the employee at the time of the earlier termination, resignation, or separation.

Separately, Labor Code § 247.5 requires an employer to keep, for at least three years, records documenting the hours worked and the paid sick days accrued and used by an employee, to allow the Labor Commissioner access to those records, and to make them available to the employee in the same manner as other wage-statement-related records; if an employer does not maintain adequate records, the statute presumes the employee is entitled to the maximum number of accruable hours under the Act, unless the employer rebuts that presumption with clear and convincing evidence. Section 247.5 also states that, notwithstanding any other provision of the Act, an employer is not obligated to inquire into or record the specific purpose for which an employee uses paid leave or paid time off.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code § 245.5's definition of "employee," for purposes of this Act, excludes five categories of workers. The first is an employee covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement that expressly provides for wages, hours, and working conditions; expressly provides paid sick days (or a paid leave or paid time off policy permitting sick-day use) and final and binding arbitration of disputes over those provisions; and provides premium overtime rates and a regular hourly rate at least 30 percent above the state minimum wage — except that this exclusion does not reach the specific victim-of-violence-related permitted use described elsewhere in this Act. The second is a construction-industry employee covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement meeting similar wage and overtime conditions, where the agreement either predates January 1, 2015, or expressly and unambiguously waives this Act's requirements. The third is an air carrier flight deck or cabin crew member covered by Title II of the federal Railway Labor Act, so long as the individual receives compensated time off equal to or exceeding this Act's own default accrual amount. The fourth is a state or local public retiree drawing a retirement allowance who returns to work without reinstatement into the applicable public retirement system. The fifth is an employee as defined in a specified provision of the federal Railway Labor Act, 45 U.S.C. § 351(d).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 245.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, qualifying collective-bargaining-agreement exclusion
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (d) of Section 246.5, an employee covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement if the agreement expressly provides for the wages, hours of work, and working conditions of employees, and expressly provides for paid sick days or a paid leave or paid time off policy that permits the use of sick days for those employees, final and binding arbitration of disputes concerning the application of its paid sick days provisions, premium wage rates for all overtime hours worked, and regular hourly rate of pay of not less than 30 percent more than the state minimum wage rate.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 245.5(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, construction-industry collective-bargaining-agreement exclusion
citations.quote: An employee in the construction industry covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement if the agreement expressly provides for the wages, hours of work, and working conditions of employees, premium wage rates for all overtime hours worked, and regular hourly pay of not less than 30 percent more than the state minimum wage rate, and the agreement either (A) was entered into before January 1, 2015, or (B) expressly waives the requirements of this article in clear and unambiguous terms. For purposes of this subparagraph, “employee in the construction industry” means an employee performing work associated with construction, including work involving alteration, demolition, building, excavation, renovation, remodeling, maintenance, improvement, repair work, and any other work as described by Chapter 9 (commencing with Section 7000) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code, and other similar or related occupations or trades.

citations.quote: An individual employed by an air carrier as a flight deck or cabin crew member that is subject to Title II of the federal Railway Labor Act (45 U.S.C. Sec. 151 et seq.), provided that the individual is provided with compensated time off equal to or exceeding the amount established in paragraph (1) of subdivision (b) of Section 246.

citations.quote: An employee of the state, city, county, city and county, district, or any other public entity who is a recipient of a retirement allowance and employed without reinstatement into the employee’s respective retirement system pursuant to either Article 8 (commencing with Section 21220) of Chapter 12 of Part 3 of Division 5 of Title 2 of the Government Code, or Article 8 (commencing with Section 31670) of Chapter 3 of Part 3 of Division 4 of Title 3 of the Government Code.
